title: Who really got rich in the California Gold Rush?
subject: histoire
description: On January 24, 1848, a carpenter scooped a few yellow flecks out of a sawmill channel and set off the biggest rush in history. But the real winners hardly ever held a pan.
author: elizabeth-singer-hunt

hero.hook: Thousands of men dug through freezing mud for a few flecks of gold: the fortune was waiting behind the counter.

blocks.text: On **January 24, 1848**, James Marshall, a carpenter from New Jersey, was inspecting the sawmill he was building at Coloma, on the American River, for a landowner named [[John Sutter]]. In the tailrace, he spotted bright yellow flecks. He pounded them with a rock, and the cook, Jennie Wimmer, boiled them in lye: they flattened and did not tarnish.

After further tests, the two men concluded that Marshall really had "found a gold mine." That day opened the California Gold Rush: years of mass migration, cultures from all over the world thrown together, the foundations of one of the largest economies on the planet. But who, exactly, came out of it rich?

sections.title: Gold fever spreads around the world

blocks.text: Sutter and Marshall wanted to keep the secret. But Jennie Wimmer and her sons started talking. At the same time, gold flecks were being used to pay for goods at a store at Sutter's Fort, run by a partner of a merchant and newspaper publisher, [[Sam Brannan]]. Brannan quickly stocked his shelves with mining gear.

Then he advertised the news by shouting "Gold!" in the streets of San Francisco. In **December 1848**, President James K. Polk publicly confirmed the discovery. From then on, the whole world could not stop talking, and dreaming, about striking it rich in California.

From **1848 to 1855**, roughly **300,000** people emigrated to California to look for gold or to seize the opportunities the rush created. About **100,000** arrived in 1849 alone: they became known as the [[Forty-Niners]]. Most came from the United States, others from Latin America, Europe, Australia, Polynesia and China.

blocks.caption: "The Way They Go to California" (1849), a satirical lithograph by Nathaniel Currier.

blocks.text: Getting there could be deadly. Overland from the East Coast meant at least **3,000 miles** of extreme weather, cholera and dwindling supplies. By sea, travelers spent four to six months sailing around [[Cape Horn]], roughly **17,000 miles**. A shorter route crossed the [[Isthmus of Panama]], where yellow fever and malaria waited, before another ship carried them north to San Francisco.

In 1846, before the Gold Rush, the Donner-Reed Party took an untested shortcut to California and became trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada. Forty of the 87 travelers died. Some survivors resorted to cannibalism before rescue parties reached them in 1847.

In San Francisco, other challenges were waiting. The cost of living was exorbitant, and the gold fields lay another **100 miles** to the north. Those who made it to one of the roughly **500 mining camps** found dangerous, exhausting work: hours standing in freezing river water, swirling a wash pan and hoping gold would settle to the bottom.

blocks.caption: Miners, several of them Chinese, in front of a long tom at Auburn Ravine in 1852.

blocks.text: When the river deposits dried up, miners had to "coyote": dig a vertical shaft with tunnels radiating from it, which threatened to collapse on them or poison them as they hunted for gold. For most miners, striking it rich remained a dream. The majority of those who really made money never mined at all.

Not everything the Gold Rush touched turned to gold. California's Native population collapsed: killings, disease, starvation, displacement. Mining also released millions of pounds of toxic mercury that still contaminate the state's rivers today.

Sam Brannan, for his part, never dug. While thousands of prospectors were chasing their fortune, he became California's first millionaire by selling them supplies. Between **May 1 and July 10, 1848**, his store at Sutter's Fort took in **$36,000** worth of gold as payment for goods.

blocks.caption: Samuel Brannan, merchant and publisher, California's first millionaire.

blocks.text: Others did the same. In **1853**, Levi Strauss built a dry-goods business that eventually gave rise to Levi's jeans. [[Wells Fargo]] was founded in **1852** to carry the miners' gold and mail. In 1849, Domingo Ghirardelli opened a general store, complete with his now-famous chocolate, and the Canton Restaurant became one of the first Chinese restaurants in America. For those who wanted to get rich quick, the real vein was to "mine the miners."

events.title: The rush runs out of steam
events.detail: Around 300,000 people have emigrated to California since 1848.

blocks.text: On **September 9, 1850**, California became the 31st state of the United States, with "Eureka!", "I have found it!", as its motto. In an ironic twist, John Sutter, the man whose land gave birth to the Gold Rush, died in poverty. So did James Marshall and Sam Brannan, despite their pivotal roles in California's boom.
The Gold Rush mostly enriched the people who sold shovels, cloth and transport to the gold seekers: the real mine was the miners.
